entries.title: Flydubai pilot investigated over possible attempt to crash Tel Aviv-bound flight
entries.summary: Israeli media say authorities are investigating whether a Flydubai pilot tried to crash an Israel-bound plane before it diverted to Saudi Arabia.
entries.content:
Israel

Flydubai pilot investigated over possible crash attempt

September 30, 2026

Israeli media say authorities are investigating whether a Flydubai pilot tried to crash an Israel-bound plane before it diverted to Saudi Arabia.

Authorities are investigating whether a pilot on a Flydubai flight tried to crash a Tel Aviv-bound on Wednesday, according to Israeli media reports.

The plane lost thousands of meters of altitude in about a minute before making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, with Flydubai confirming that all passengers were safe.

What happened on the Flydubai flight?

Flydubai said flight FZ 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv experienced an "incident" while en route and landed safely at Tabuk Airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia. The aircraft was a Boeing 737 MAX 8.

"The aircraft has landed safely in Tabuk Airport and all passengers are safe and accounted for," a Flydubai spokesperson said.

Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported that authorities were investigating whether one of the pilots had deliberately tried to crash the aircraft, with the other pilot intervening to stop him.

Israeli media said one of the pilots suffered a stab wound. Initial reports had described the incident only as a fight between the two pilots.

The Israeli news portal Ynet reported that the aircraft entered a steep descent and that passengers helped one pilot prevent the other from crashing the plane.



Images published by Israeli outlets appeared to show a passenger with blood on his shirt.

Different outlets have given different nationalities for the pilot and co-pilot, with some saying one was Russian and the other Ukrainian, while others state they were Omani and Emirati.

Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 initially showed a second Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, FZ1081, diverting back toward Dubai. It later showed the aircraft continuing toward Tel Aviv. There was no immediate explanation from Flightradar24 for the change.

How far did the plane fall?

Flight tracking data shows the aircraft suddenly losing around half its altitude as it neared Saudi Arabia's border with Jordan.

The plane dropped from nearly 34,000 feet (10,360 meters) at 05:21 GMT/UTC to below 17,000 feet (5,180 meters) at 05:22 GMT/UTC, according to Flightradar data.

Israel's Kan public broadcaster and Channel 12 reported that the Israeli military scrambled fighter jets amid initial fears of a possible hijacking. That possibility was later dismissed, according to the reports.

What have Israeli authorities said?

An unnamed senior Israeli government official told Channel 12 that a major disaster had been averted.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said he had held consultations over the incident and was monitoring developments.

"The incident is under control, and all measures are currently being deployed in order to return the Israeli passengers safely to Israel," his office said.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Is US President Donald Trump right to rename AI as 'Super Intelligence'?
entries.summary: Donald Trump thinks the name artificial intelligence sounds "fake" and has ordered US agencies to use "Super Intelligence" instead. Yet, tech firms and researchers have little reason to play along.
entries.content:
September 30, 2026

Donald Trump thinks the name artificial intelligence sounds "fake" and has ordered US agencies to use "Super Intelligence" instead. Yet, tech firms and researchers have little reason to play along.

What's with Donald Trump and renaming things? First, the Gulf of Mexico became the Gulf of America — in US federal documents, if not globally. Then Lake Ontario became Lake America. Now he wants to rebrand the defining technology of our time: artificial intelligence (AI).

Earlier this month, the US president claimed on his Truth Social platform that the term artificial intelligence is "inaccurate" and "ineloquent." He said "superior," "extreme," or "supreme" intelligence were better alternatives.

In a three-day social media poll, Trump fans chose "Super Intelligence" (SI) by about 65% to 35% (for Superior Intelligence), allowing him to announce at the United Nations General Assembly last week that US federal documents would use his new term going forward.

'AI is not superintelligence'

The tech industry has yet to adopt the phrase, however, while academics warn that superintelligence is a future term for when technology can beat humans across the board. They say the current AI models are years away from that milestone.

"Most AI is not superintelligence — it's just different intelligence," Pedro Domingos, a computer science professor from the University of Washington, told DW. "AI is doing different things from what humans do, so calling it superintelligence is misleading."

Computer scientists and mathematicians coined the name "artificial intelligence" in 1956 at a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. "Artificial" simply meant made by humans, as opposed to natural human intelligence.

Not all experts agreed with the name. In the book "Machines Who Think," historian Pamela McCorduck cited AI pioneer Arthur Samuel, who said the term "makes you think there's something kind of phony about this."

Despite this, the name artificial intelligence has stuck for 70 years. Critics say changing it now will not quieten the many fears around AI, including job losses, human obsolescence or machines slipping out of our control.

Rebrand won't quell AI fears

"The name change is fostering these kinds of fears: 'Oh, this is superintelligence and it's going to make humans obsolete, turn on us and take our jobs'," warned Domingos. "If you want to maximize the backlash against AI, rename it Superior Intelligence."

Those public fears are growing fast. In a Public First poll for Politico earlier this month, about half of respondents in six countries — the United States, Canada, France, Spain, Germany and the United Kingdom — backed a pause in further AI development to reduce the risk that the new tech could destroy humanity.

A separate CNN/SSRS poll found nearly nine in 10 Americans are more concerned than excited about AI surpassing human intelligence.

Those concerns have already reached the US Congress. Last week, Vermont's independent Senator Bernie Sanders co-introduced a bill to "permanently ban the development of artificial superintelligence" that humans cannot control.

The legislation also calls for a pause on advanced AI development until federal testing and oversight are in place.

A branding gift to help the AI boom?

Trump's new term could, however, suit the major US AI players, who are keen to play up their advanced models. Those systems already outperform humans on many specialized tasks and until recently were far ahead of China.

Yet both Anthropic, the firm behind the Claude model, and OpenAI, which created ChatGPT, have pushed back plans to go public. Some market watchers blamed the delays on recent scares where AI models hacked into computer systems or ran tasks they were not meant to.ran tasks they were not meant to.

With Chinese models closing much of the quality gap with much less computing power, US labs may still appreciate the branding that helps confirm they are still leading the AI race. Global spending on AI is expected to surpass $1 trillion (€880 billion), according to Goldman Sachs research.

"The [US] labs have every interest in calling it super, hyper, superior and whatnot intelligence, because it's playing up their capabilities. It's like just marketing," said Domingos, the author of the 2015 book "The Master Algorithm."

Superintelligence remains a moving target

While the current AI models keep improving and can already run many tasks on their own, the next step that many labs discuss is AI systems that improve themselves. That's called recursive self-improvement or RSI.

On that journey, Elon Musk has predicted that AI learning could be automated, with limited human input, by the end of this year or 2027. OpenAI thinks it could take a year longer. But even then, AI systems won't be fully recursive.

Jürgen Schmidhuber, a German computer scientist based in Switzerland, argued in a blog post earlier this month that "full RSI, however, will require not just self-improving [AI] software but self-improving hardware in the physical world."

In other words, to reach superintelligence or RSI, tech companies would have to produce chips, humanoid robots and even replace entire factories without human input.

While AI is already speeding up chip design, it cannot yet run the foundry alone. Self-improving machines, with no human input, are likely still decades away.

Beyond the science of machine learning, politics will likely play a bigger role in whether Super Intelligence sticks. While Trump claimed Chinese President Xi Jinping liked the name, China has yet to show any signs of changing from AI.

 At a tech summit on Tuesday with key industry leaders, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government bodies and agencies to start using the term SI. While some Big Tech leaders have adopted it, experts say the new term is unlikely to catch on.

"Knowing the political orientation of most people in the [AI] field, they're more likely to have the opposite reaction, which is: 'To hell with you. We're going to call it artificial intelligence even more than before'," Domingos said.

Edited by: Rob Mudge

entries.title: Eurovision seeks to expand brand despite frictions
entries.summary: The 2026 Eurovision Song Contest was marred by boycotts in protest against Israel's participation in the midst of its war on Gaza. It still aims to keep growing.
entries.content:
Europe

Eurovision seeks to expand brand despite frictions

September 30, 2026

The 2026 Eurovision Song Contest was marred by boycotts in protest against Israel's participation in the midst of its war on Gaza. It still aims to keep growing.

"Bringing the world together through music has always been an incredibly powerful idea and has stood the test of time for 70 years," Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green told DW on the sidelines of the event's annual European Broadcasting Union (EBU) workshop held in mid-September. "And I think the more difficult the world gets around us, the more important these shows of unity, these shows of togetherness become."

While Green is intent on promoting the unity of the international music contest that celebrated its 70th anniversary in May, the 2026 event was also infamously marked by unprecedented backlash.

Political boycotts over Israel's inclusion amid the war in Gaza led to a significant low point in participation and viewership, dropping from 166 million viewers in 2025 down to 131 million viewers a year later.

The 2027 song contest is set to remain affected by geopolitics.

Of the five countries which boycotted the 2026 event — the Netherlands, Spain, Iceland, Slovenia and Ireland — the latter has already confirmed that it will not participate for the second time in a row.

The Netherlands' usual Eurovision broadcaster had also announced it would be snubbing the show again, stating it refused to take part in an event that "can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict." Now, Dutch public broadcasting association NPO decided to step in and resume participation in the contest.

The three other countries that pulled out in 2026 have yet to make an official announcement for 2027.

Broadcasters have until mid-October 2026 to withdraw their application without facing a financial penalty.

Some adjustments made amid the crisis

In August, the contest organizers announced new rules, according to which "the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region," they said in a statement.

The winning country usually earns the right to host the following edition, though the United Kingdom hosted the 2023 event on behalf of Ukraine due to Russia's war on Ukraine. Even though the rule doesn't name the country, it clearly aims to avoid having the show held in Israel, which came close to taking home the trophy in 2025 and 2026.

Organizers also plan to introduce changes to reduce politically motivated voting.

The current system allows viewers to vote up to 10 times per payment method for their favorite act, by phone, text message or online.

There was a huge uproar in 2025 when the Israeli government encouraged Israelis to register multiple votes for its contestant. The controversy had already led to a change in the voting rules; the maximum number of public votes was halved from 20 to 10.

Now the plan is to move the vote entirely online, with a system that would require people to select three acts instead of one.

Bulgaria already at work for 2027

Since Bulgarian singer Dara won in Vienna with her song "Bangaranga," her country will be hosting the event next year.

The competition will take place in Burgas, a city on the Black Sea coast.

When the city's selection was announced, people in Burgas celebrated with spontaneous music and dance performances and flash mobs, said Milena Milotinova, general director of Bulgaria's public broadcaster BNT, host of the televised event.

"I'm glad that people in Bulgaria are actually so passionate about Eurovision," Milotinova told DW. "This will be the first time Bulgaria has organized such a large-scale event at such a high level."

The Balkan country participated for the first time in 2005. It now needs to quickly develop its infrastructure for the international event.

"The important thing is that we already have a hall, and the stage design is being developed based on that," said Milotinova.

"We are in the midst of frantic preparations," she added. "There are no days off, so we hope we'll be able to get everything done on time and put on a spectacular, world-class Eurovision show."

Expanding the Eurovision brand

Beyond blows to the contest's viewership, Eurovision also had to deal with a substantial financial setback due to the withdrawal of Spain, which was traditionally one of the so-called "big five" contributors supporting the event.

Yet amid these challenges, Eurovision organizers are working to expand the brand's international reach.

The Eurovision Song Contest Asia will debut in November this year, with Thailand's capital Bangkok selected as the host city for its inaugural edition. Eleven countries are taking part, and negotiations are underway to get more Asian countries to join in 2027.

A Latin American spin-off of the format has been announced in the past but has not yet materialized.

"We're always investigating new areas of the world that we can take the show to," said Martin Green. "We're beavering away on all sorts of ideas."

Canada joins the party

One achievement organizers are definitely celebrating is Canada's addition to the European lineup, which was announced in July: "We are so happy that the Canadians chose to join our family," said the Eurovision Song Contest director.

Participation is not restricted to Europe's geographic boundaries; it's open to active members of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU). Israel's public broadcaster has competed regularly since 1973. Due to its massive fan base, Australia first joined as a special participant in 2015 and has remained a committed contestant since.

"We're learning about what this takes, but we're going to put our best foot forward and really show the world what Canada can do," Jennifer Dettman, Canada's Eurovision Song Contest head of delegation, told DW.

The participation also marks a strategic push by Prime Minister Mark Carney's government to deepen cultural and diplomatic ties with Europe. His government's budget included $150 million Canadian (€93 million, $106 million) in funding for the broadcaster.

"This is the biggest global music event. So it's an opportunity to put our artists on this global stage," added Dettman. "People are really excited to do that."

Jakov Leon conducted the interviews.

Edited by: Sarah Hucal

entries.title: South Korea: Lost shark draws over half a million visitors
entries.summary: The South Korean port of Busan says that a stranded shark has become a major tourist draw. It's also named the ocean predator an honorary ambassador to the city.
entries.content:
South Korea

South Korea: Lost shark draws over half a million visitors

September 30, 2026

The South Korean port of Busan says that a stranded shark has become a major tourist draw. It's also named the ocean predator an honorary ambassador to the city.

A shark stranded in a canal in the northern port city of Busan has become South Korea's latest celebrity, tourist magnet and ambassador, as authorities' attempts to guide it back out to sea have so far faltered. 

What do we know about the stranded shark?

The shark was first spotted in a narrow waterway in Busan's North Port on September 18.

Reports on its possible species vary but seem to suggest it's a type of requiem shark, possibly a bull shark or a bronze whaler.

It's a fairly large shark, appearing to be roughly 3.5 meters (around 11 feet, 6 inches) long.

It's been nicknamed "Bukangi," derived from the Korean name for the North Port in Busan, Buk Hang.

Trapped aquatic tourist trap

Busan city authorities say roughly 600,000 people have flocked to see the creature over the past two weeks.

During the four-day Chuseok bank holiday weekend, Busan city authorities said that almost half a million people visited the waterfront park where the shark was stranded, compared to an average of around 2,000 visitors on weekends.

City Mayor Chun Jae-soo thanked the involuntary visitor for publicity that would otherwise have cost "trillions."

Local media reported a spike in sales of shark-shaped ice creams at nearby stores.

The city named the lost predator an honorary ambassador after 91% of participants in a social media poll approved of the notion.

Shares in the Pinkfong Company, the studio behind the viral "Baby Shark" song, also rose by around 7% at one point amid the hype.

The excitement has also led to false rumors of a second sighting, or even of it being the shark's own spawn, with AI-generated dross inevitably following.

How are authorities trying to guide it back out to sea?

A rescue operation earlier this week failed.

The Coast Guard and other agencies deployed vessels that sprayed jets of water behind the shark, trying to encourage it to swim back towards the ocean.

Instead the shark simply evaded the streams without heading in the desired direction.

South Korea's Chosun Daily newspaper reported that a fresh attempt, this time seeking to use a net to guide the shark out, was being planned for Friday.

The shark is the latest unlikely animal celebrity craze to grip South Korea, not least following the excitement in April over Neukgu, a young wolf that escaped from a zoo. It spent nine days at large before being recaptured.

The incident is also somewhat reminiscent of the German frenzy this year over a beached humpback whale, who was in turn given the place-based nickname of "Timmy" — after the Timmendorfer Strand beach on the Baltic coast, the site of its first stranding. 

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Eiffel Tower chief Patrick Branco Ruivo to step down after female staff excluded during Hindu group's visit
entries.summary: An investigation found management failures led to female Eiffel Tower staff being excluded during a Hindu group's visit.
entries.content:
France

Eiffel Tower chief to quit over exclusion of female staff

September 30, 2026

An investigation found management failures led to female Eiffel Tower staff being excluded during a Hindu group's visit.

The head of the company that operates the Eiffel Tower is set to step down at the end of the year after female staff were excluded during a visit by a Hindu religious group in September.

An independent investigation found a series of failures surrounding the incident, which prompted Eiffel Tower staff to strike and drew criticism from French politicians.

What happened at the Eiffel Tower?

Patrick Branco Ruivo, director general of the Societe d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), will leave the position he has held since late 2018.

The company said an independent investigation into the September 5 visit had uncovered a series of operational failures that resulted in female employees being excluded.

It described the situation as "unacceptable."

Management had instructed female employees not to come into contact with a delegation from Bochasanwasi Shri Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), a Hindu religious organization.

The company initially acknowledged that withdrawing female staff from the tower's third floor during the group's visit had been a mistake.

What has the Hindu group said?

BAPS denied asking for female employees to be removed or hidden during the visit.

"The religious practices of our monks were explained to the Eiffel Tower's management in advance. These are personal spiritual commitments, which our monks observe without seeking to impose them on others. They do not require women to be excluded from the places they visit," BAPS said.

BAPS is an international religious and civic organization within the Swaminarayan tradition of Hinduism. The delegation was in the region for celebrations connected with the inauguration of a traditional Hindu stone temple.

What happens now?

The incident led Eiffel Tower employees to strike on September 7, forcing the landmark to close for a day.

SETE chair Ariel Weil said the company would introduce measures and training programs aimed at promoting gender equality.

The German account also says a separate protocol department will be established following the investigation.

The 330-meter (1,083-foot) Eiffel Tower attracts around 7 million visitors annually.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: India news: Key opposition leaders meet to discuss poll body row
entries.summary: India's opposition leaders meet in New Delhi to push back against voter roll revisions and discuss poll body chief Gyanesh Kumar. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: Opposition meets over poll body row

Published September 30, 2026last updated September 30, 2026

India's opposition leaders meet in New Delhi to push back against voter roll revisions and discuss poll body chief Gyanesh Kumar. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here are the latest developments we are following from India on Wednesday, September 30:

  • India opposition bloc meets, demands roll back of voter list revision
  • Security stepped up near Ujjain mosque after clashes
  • What is Delhi's latest action plan to tackle winter smog?

Skip next section INDIA bloc plans 'Save Democracy' marches over SIR, starting October 2

INDIA bloc plans 'Save Democracy' marches over SIR, starting October 2

The INDIA bloc has announced a "Save Democracy " march as leaders of the opposition alliance met on Wednesday to mull a joint strategy over the issue of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls.

India bloc leaders will hold nationwide protest marches from October 2 to 8 at the district level, while all opposition MPs will march to the Election Commission on October 6, Congress party President Mallikarjun Kharge told a press briefing after the meeting.

The meeting, which lasted over three hours, included Congress' Rahul Gandhi, All India Trinamool Congress party (TMC) chief Mamata Banerjee, Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, among leaders from other opposition parties.

Banerjee, who is the former chief minister of West Bengal, told the media that the opposition would continue its protest till Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigns. She also called for the resignation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Gandhi said the INDIA bloc was committed to ensuring that those, who he alleged, have "destroyed" India's democracy were "punished".

The bloc's leaders also announced a major rally in the Indian capital on November 1, where they would raise issues related to alleged "vote theft".

Gandhi earlier posted on X, accusing Modi of using India's poll body chief Kumar "to steal elections".

The INDIA bloc on Wednesday also demanded that all cases linked to the SIR that are in the Supreme Court should be resolved "as soon as possible".

Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has accused the opposition of "misleading" the public on the SIR and of an "attack" India's constitutional bodies.

Skip next section Apple pay debuts in India

Apple pay debuts in India

Apple on Wednesday introduced its payment service in India as it taps into the lucrative digital payments market in the world’s most populous nation. 

Apple Pay is now available for Indian users across iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch, a statement from the US multinational corporation said, adding that support for Mac computers was coming soon. 

The launch comes in partnership with India's Axis Bank, which is the country's third-largest private lender.

Customers of Axis Bank will be able to store their credit cards on Apple wallets and "use them at thousands of in-store and online merchants across India," Apple said.

Apple Pay has also held talks with the larger HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank but is yet to agree commercial terms, according to news agency Reuters.

In India, over 80% of digital payments are handled through the homegrown United Payments Interface (UPI), which is also the world's largest real-time payments system in terms of volume, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

"India is home to a dynamic and digitally savvy population that continues to embrace a cashless future while expecting the highest standards of security and privacy, and we're so excited to bring Apple Pay to users in India today," Jennifer Bailey, Apple's vice president of Apple Pay and Apple Wallet, said.

Skip next section Security tightened in Ujjain after mosque demolition clashes

Security tightened in Ujjain after mosque demolition clashes

Security was tightened Wednesday around the Shahi Masjid in Ujjain, in the central Indian state of Madhya Pradesh, after clashes over the demolition of part of the historic mosque for road-widening work ahead of a 2028 Hindu pilgrimage.

On Monday, tensions flared in the central Indian city as a large crowd gathered to oppose the proposed partial demolition and allegedly threw stones. Police fired tear gas shells to disperse the crowd.

According to Indian media reports, 15 people have been detained so far over the violence.

Authorities said the situation was peaceful Wednesday, with more than 2,500 police personnel deployed across Ujjain.

The Madhya Pradesh High Court had earlier disposed of a petition over the dispute after representatives of the mosque and civic authorities agreed on a compromise.

On Tuesday, news agency ANI cited Ujjain District Collector Roshan Kumar Singh as saying the mosque committee was itself removing the portion affected by the road-widening project.

The road-widening is taking place ahead of a Hindu fair called Simhastha, which is slated to be held in 2028 and is expected to attract millions of devotees.

Skip next section Eiffel Tower chief to quit over exclusion of female staff during Hindu group visit

Eiffel Tower chief to quit over exclusion of female staff during Hindu group visit

The head of the company that operates the Eiffel Tower is set to step down at the end of the year after female staff were excluded during a visit by a Hindu religious group in September. 

Patrick Branco Ruivo, director general of the Societe d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), will leave the position he has held since late 2018.

The company said an independent investigation into the September 5 visit had uncovered a series of operational failures that resulted in female employees being excluded.

It described the situation as "unacceptable."

Management had instructed female employees not to come into contact with a delegation from Bochasanwasi Shri Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), a Hindu religious organization which has its headquarters in Ahmedabad in the Indian state of Gujarat.

BAPS denied asking for female employees to be removed or hidden during the visit.

The incident led Eiffel Tower employees to strike on September 7, forcing the landmark to close for a day.

Read full report here.

Skip next section India opposition leaders push back against voter roll review

India opposition leaders push back against voter roll review

A meeting of the INDIA bloc, the Congress-led alliance of opposition parties, is underway at the Constitution Club in New Delhi on Wednesday, where opposition leaders are expected to discuss the Election Commission of India's (ECI) Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists and the furor surrounding India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, that has gripped the nation in recent days.

Mallikarjun Kharge, the president of India's main opposition Congress party, called for the roll back of the SIR, a hotly debated exercise to verify hundreds of millions of Indian voters, that began last year.

Kharge said that the "ballot belongs to the people" and the principle of "one, person, one vote, one value" in Indian democracy was under a "serious threat."

"It is shocking that as many as 13.3 Crore (133 million) voters have blatantly been removed from voter list. Their power to take part in a DEMOCRACY has been snatched. It is ordinary voters who should be deciding who comes to power rather than those who are in power," he said.

Why India's poll body chief is under scrutiny

Wednesday's meeting comes after an investigative report by the Indian Express published last week said that there were differences within the Election Commission of India over decisions related to the SIR.

The report stirred a political storm, with protests calling for the resignation of the poll body's chief, Gyanesh Kumar, for allegedly undermining the ECI's credibility.

According to the Indian Express, Kumar's fellow election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months regarding voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral-roll data, but those concerns were not taken into consideration.

The report said that in one objection, one of the commissioners complained that the ECI acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."

The ECI has deemed all its decisions lawful, saying that differing views were a routine "part of decision-making."

The three-member commission, comprising Kumar, Sandhu and Joshi, oversees the SIR, which the poll body says removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also prevents the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

However, opposition parties and critics allege that the exercise has gone beyond that remit and removed millions of eligible voters to the benefit of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Congress demands CEC Kumar's resignation

On Wednesday, Kharge also called for the removal or resignation of Kumar, saying that there could be no credible election without an "independent and impartial" election body.

He said that the ECI head's "very integrity" and "intentions" were under question.

Last week, Congress carried out demonstrations across the country demanding Kumar's resignation.

Pressure group Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), which claims millions of supporters, said that it would launch nationwide protests on October 2 if Kumar does not step down.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, back with the Wednesday roundup of the biggest headlines capturing India's attention.

Residents of the Indian capital, who have been waking up to cooler mornings, are discussing whether winter will arrive early. But apart from the nip in the air, there is also growing concern about the winter smog that chokes Delhi in the waning months of the year. The city, however, is trying to stay ahead of the smog with a winter action plan that includes construction curbs, vehicle restrictions and work-from-home arrangements.

In political news, opposition leaders from the INDIA bloc are meeting in New Delhi for a key meeting where they will discuss a joint response to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) row surrounding the country's poll body and calls for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.

In sports news, Indian archers have struck gold twice. India's compound mixed team and women's team have both won gold medals.

We will cover these and other stories in this blog.

entries.title: Germany news: Cabinet approves care reform bill
entries.summary: The German Cabinet has approved a draft bill on reforming the care system after long debate. Police have launched raids across Germany targeting Hells Angels gangs and a money-laundering network. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Cabinet approves care reform bill

Published September 30, 2026last updated September 30, 2026

The German Cabinet has approved a draft bill on reforming the care system after long debate. Police have launched raids across Germany targeting Hells Angels gangs and a money-laundering network. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • A package of care system reforms has been approved by the Cabinet
  • Police have raided sites in Germany and other European countries in a crackdown on Hells Angels bikers and a money-laundering network
  • All trains stations in Germany are to be (almost) no-alcohol zones from October

This is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, September 30, 2026:

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your preferred source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.

Skip next section Unknown Christmas work by Humperdinck discovered

Unknown Christmas work by Humperdinck discovered

A "Christmas Lullaby" by composer Engelbert Humperdinck (1854-1921) donated by his great-grandson to his birth city of Siegburg has been confirmed to be a previously unknown work.

"For the music world, the find is a sensation," city spokesman Jan Gerull told the DPA news agency.

The one-page manuscript with the work for four-voice male choir was given to the Siegburg city archive by Humperdinck's great-grandson, Lothar Witte, some time ago for its collection related to the composer.

The head of the Musicwerkstatt Siegburg, Christian Ubber, said it had first had to be clarified whether Humperdinck had used and published the work in another context.

"This examination took some time and turned out negative so that it is only now certain that this 'Christmas Lullaby' was really unknown up to now," he said.

According to city spokesman Gerull, the piece, a highly indivualized version of the German Christmas song "Josef lieber, Josef mein," is not easy to sing owing to the composer's sometimes complex style.

But, he said, this had not dampened the enthusiasm.

"Siegburg is looking forward to having the piece performed before Christmas," he said.

Skip next section Cabinet gives green light to care system reform package

Cabinet gives green light to care system reform package

The German Cabinet has put its seal of approval on a draft bill put forward by Health Minister Carsten Linnemann on reforming the care system.

The proposed reforms, which will now be put before the parliament, seek to prevent an estimated shortfall of some €8-10 million ($9 to $11 million) next year.

The reforms were the subject of heated debate between the conservative bloc of Christian Democrats (CDU), to which Linnemann belongs, and its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU), and the junior coalition party the Social Democrats (SPD).

The draft bill builds largely on proposals by former Health Minister Nina Warken, also from the CDU.

No details on the exact content of the bill as it now stands have been released.

Skip next section Bundeswehr failing to tackle sexual harassment — report

Bundeswehr failing to tackle sexual harassment — report

The German armed forces are doing too little to crack down on instances of sexual offenses against women in their ranks, according to public service broadcaster ARD.

This comes as the Bundeswehr is actively seeking to recruit women.

Witnesses and victims of such offenses told the ARD's news magazine REPORT MAINZ that many personnel were scared to report what had happened to them for fear of negative career consequences.

The number of suspected cases of sexual harassment has been rising every year, with 413 reported in 2024 and 472 in 2025, but the number of unreported cases is likely high, according to the ARD.

A spokeswoman from the Defense Ministry told REPORT MAINZ that there had been an "disproportionate rise" in reports of sexual offenses this year.

Women have been permitted to join the Bundeswehr in all capacities for 25 years but still make up just 13.6% of personnel.

The Defense Ministry has, however, rejected the claim by a military historian in the program that the integration of women in the Bundeswehr had so far failed.

Women in the Bundeswehr were "accepted and respected," and there was no "value and rights free space for any group of people" in the German armed forces, it said.

Skip next section Cabinet debates care reform after uncertainty

Cabinet debates care reform after uncertainty

The German Cabinet is to discuss the draft bill put forward by Health Minister Carsten Linnemann to reform the care system after much heated debate between the coalition partners, the Federal Press Office in Berlin has said.

The reform proposals have highlighted divisions between the bloc of conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) with Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU), and junior coalition partner the center-left Social Democrats (SPD).

Those divisions made it uncertain up to the last moment whether Wednesday's meeting was to take place.

Skip next section Police raid Hells Angels sites in Germany and elsewhere

Police raid Hells Angels sites in Germany and elsewhere

More than 1,000 police officers have launched raids in Germany and other European countries targeting Hells Angels bikers and an associated money-laundering network.

Duisburg police said the officers would execute a number of arrest warrants and confiscate up to €48.6 million ($55.15 million) of illicit funds.

More than 100 locations were to be searched, with 71 people under investigation.

Searches are being carried out in the states of North Rhine-Westphalia, Rhineland-Palatinate, Baden-Württemberg, Berlin and Bavaria, as well as in Belgium, Bulgaria and the Netherlands.

According to police, those under investigation are suspected of "forming a criminal association, predatory and commercial blackmail, gang and commercial fraud and commercial money-laundering."

They are also believed to be behind weapons offenses, physical assault and tax avoidance.

The operation is under the supervision of state prosecutors in Duisburg, with the involvement of the State Office for Combating Financial Criminality in North Rhine-Westphalia (LBF).

Skip next section Coalition in race to put care reform debate to rest

Coalition in race to put care reform debate to rest

A package of reforms to Germany's care system put forward by conservative Health Minister Carsten Linnemann remains a source of contention within the coalition.

It remained unclear early on Wednesday whether a planned morning Cabinet meeting to agree on the package called by Linnemann would take place.

The junior coalition partner, the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), opposes any cuts to care services.

Among other things, it has called for a cap on personal contributions to care in retirement homes and financial adjustments to make the division fairer between private and statutory nursing care insurance models.

Both ideas have met with skepticism from Linnemann.

The reform of the system has been made necessary by the growing number of people needing care as the population ages, which has raised costs.

The National Association of Statutory Health Insurance Funds (GKV), which also represents care insurance institutes, estimates a shortfall of €4.4 billion ($5 billion) this year, and €10 billion in 2027.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom on the still-running-but-just Rhine River in Bonn!

The conservative/center-left coalition government is still quibbling over proposed reforms to Germany's care system, with time running out to reach a deal.

It remains to be seen whether the Cabinet will be in a position to approve the package on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, police have targeted a money-laundering network and biker gangs in raids.

And from October, alcohol at all German train stations will only be allowed to be consumed in restaurants

Read on for more on these and other stories.

entries.title: El Nino is a 'postcard from the future' — and could cause 451,000 excess heat deaths
entries.summary: The current El Nino could cause 451,000 excess heat deaths. Researchers warn it offers a glimpse of temperatures that may become normal within 20 years.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

El Nino: A deadly 'postcard from the future'

September 30, 2026

The current El Nino could cause 451,000 excess heat deaths. Researchers warn it offers a glimpse of temperatures that may become normal within 20 years.

Peruvian fishermen gave El Nino its name — "the little boy" or Christ Child — after noticing unusually warm Pacific waters around Christmas that caused the fish they depended on to suddenly become scarce.

But what those fishermen observed locally can have consequences thousands of kilometers away. El Nino can shift temperature and rainfall patterns around the world, bringing extreme heat and drought to some regions and heavy rain and flooding to others.

Researchers now estimate that the unusually high temperatures linked to the current El Nino could cause around 451,000 excess deaths worldwide from June 2026 to February 2027.

The event is a "postcard from the future," Tamma Carleton, head of research at the University of Chicago's Climate Impact Lab, told DW. Land temperatures over the coming months are forecast to run about 1.2 degrees C (2.1 F) above normal.

"For the average person, that's roughly the warming climate change is projected to bring about 20 years from now, arriving all at once," Carleton said.

How does El Nino affect weather worldwide?

Normally, winds blowing west across the Pacific push warm surface water towards Asia and Australia, allowing colder water to rise near South America. During El Nino, which occurs erratically every two to seven years, those winds weaken. Less cold water then rises, and much more of the Pacific stays unusually warm.

The warmer water heats the air above it and fuels rainfall over the central and eastern Pacific. The rising air spreads high in the atmosphere, sending waves that disrupt weather worldwide.

"It is like throwing a stone into a lake," climate researcher Fred Kucharski told DW. "Initially the surface perturbation is local, but then the energy spreads all over the lake through wave propagation."

Kucharski said the effects can cross the tropics within one week and reach higher latitudes in about two. Where the waves travel determines whether a region becomes hotter, cooler, wetter or drier.

The current El Nino developed in June and has strengthened rapidly since. It is now on course to become an exceptionally strong — sometimes called "super" — El Nino.

The Climate Impact Lab says its estimate covers only the first nine months of El Nino, as far as the current seasonal forecasts allow. The event is expected to continue into Northern Hemisphere spring, and its effect on global temperatures could last longer.

"We expect the final number to be meaningfully higher than what we are currently reporting here," Carleton said.

Why can El Nino be so deadly?

The estimate of 451,000 excess deaths covers deaths linked to the direct health effects of unusually high temperatures associated with El Nino.

Extreme heat strains the heart and kidneys, makes it harder for the body to maintain a safe temperature and can worsen cardiovascular, respiratory and other illnesses. As a result, the underlying condition is often recorded as the cause of death rather than the heat that aggravated it.

"Most heat deaths never show up in official statistics as heat deaths," Carleton said.

El Nino can also alter rainfall, contributing to drought in some regions and heavy rain and flooding in others. 

Floods can kill, contaminate drinking water and spread disease. Drought can damage harvests and cause water and food shortages.

Deaths from these other indirect effects are not included in the 451,000 projection.

Where will the toll be greatest?

The Climate Impact Lab expects some of the largest increases in deaths in the Sahel, South and Southeast Asia and parts of Latin America. The highest numbers of fatalities are predicted for Nigeria, Sudan, Niger, Chad, India, Indonesia and Brazil.

Many are projected to occur between December and February, meaning much of the expected toll still lies ahead.

"Heat headlines usually focus on Europe and North America," Carleton said. "This event's toll is overwhelmingly in lower-income, already-hot countries, where people have the fewest ways to adapt and where these deaths are least likely to be counted."

Are these lives being significantly shortened?

Some people who die during extreme heat are already frail. This raises an important question: Is the heat cutting their lives substantially short, or merely bringing forward deaths that would have occurred days or weeks later — an effect known as mortality displacement?

The underlying research uses annual rather than daily death rates, which largely filters out deaths brought forward by only days or weeks.

Ben Armstrong, an emeritus professor at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said he could not verify the 451,000 figure. But because the estimate is based on annual mortality data, it largely excludes deaths brought forward by only days or weeks. If the figure is correct, he said, most of those counted "would have lived at least six months longer."

Why predict deaths before they happen?

Scientists have long estimated the death toll from extreme temperatures retrospectively. Better seasonal forecasting is increasingly allowing researchers to look ahead instead.

To produce the estimate, researchers used earlier work showing how death rates change during hot weather in different parts of the world. They combined it with seasonal forecasts showing how hot each place is expected to become.

"Putting the two together lets us estimate the human cost of this event while there's still time to do something about it, rather than counting the deaths after the fact," Carleton said.

Heat warnings, cooling centers and hydration stations, home visits to vulnerable people, protections for outdoor workers and additional health care capacity could all reduce mortality.

The researchers believe targeted interventions could save tens of thousands of lives.

For Carleton, the forecast is a warning to prepare now for the heat that climate change could make commonplace.

"This El Nino gives us a look at future weather in the 2040s," Carleton said. "These temperatures will become normal in 20 years, giving us time and reason to begin investing in adaptive capacity now."

Edited: Carla Bleiker

entries.title: US troops exit Iraq after more than a decade
entries.summary: The current deployment began in 2014 in an effort to combat 'Islamic State' extremists. Iran, which has sought a complete removal of the US military from the Middle East, celebrated the withdrawal.
entries.content:
Middle East

US troops exit Iraq after more than a decade

September 30, 2026

The current deployment began in 2014 in an effort to combat 'Islamic State' extremists. Iran, which has sought a complete removal of the US military from the Middle East, celebrated the withdrawal.

After more than ten years, US forces are to withdraw from their remaining military bases in Iraq on Wednesday.

"Today, the United States and our Coalition partners formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq, consistent with the September 2024 US-Iraq joint statement and US national interests," the Pentagon said in a statement.

The Pentagon added that it will continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to Iraqi partners.

"This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said.

“It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship,” he said.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi declared that October 1, the day following the coalition's departure, should be celebrated as Sovereignty Day.

It is "a national occasion that affirms the completion of Iraq's path toward sovereignty and consolidates the presence of the state and its institutions," the heads of the executive, legislative and judicial branches said on Monday.

The troops were deployed in Iraq and Syria in 2014, to tackle the "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist group, which had taken over large swathes of both countries.

The IS was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, but coalition forces stayed on to battle the group's remnants.

The complete departure of US troops from Iraq comes 23 years after US-led forces toppled Saddam Hussein, triggering widespread upheaval and chaos, before the rise of IS.

Iran celebrates US withdrawal from Iraq

Iran and its allies celebrated the withdrawal of US forces, which was agreed upon in 2024 by then-US President Joe Biden. The agreement has now been executed under Donald Trump's term even as US continues to wage a war against Iran.

Iran, which wants a US-free Middle East, sees the US pullout from Iraq as a triumph for its "axis of resistance" of ​allied armed groups across the region.

The withdrawal of the US troops from Iraq has raised threats of diminished security in the region as Iran-backed Shi'ite militias are vying to gain more control and potentially regroup 'IS'.

US withdrawal leaves Kurds in Iraq anxious

The withdrawal leaves the the federal government and the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region, where most of remaining US bases operated, vulnerable.

Kurds in Erbil, capital of the Kurdistan region, told AFP news agency they are increasingly anxious about their safety from drones that have repeatedly targeted their autonomous canton, once the US air defense systems are removed.

 “The departure of the United States from the Kurdistan Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern,” the Kurdish regional government's Peshmerga Ministry said in a statement.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: 'Alternative Nobel' honors women's rights activists, AI researcher
entries.summary: The Right Livelihood Award has gone to a female AI researcher and women fighting repression. The Sweden-based prize has been dubbed an "alternative Nobel."
entries.content:
September 30, 2026

The Right Livelihood Award has gone to a female AI researcher and women fighting repression. The Sweden-based prize has been dubbed an "alternative Nobel."

A leading AI researcher, together with a woman lawyer from Pakistan and two women-led rights groups, on Wednesday received a Sweden-based rights award that honors work seen as contributing to a more just and peaceful world.

The Right Livelihood Award was created by Swedish-German philanthropist Jakob von Uexkull in 1980 to celebrate achievements in the fields of environment and international development disregarded by the Nobel Prizes.

It is usually awarded a week before the Nobel Prizes.

Right Livelihood said this year's winners, selected from 200 nominations from 72 countries, were being honored for "resistance to systems that push people to the margins, and a shared insistence on putting people back at the center."

Who won the Right Livelihood Award in 2026?

An AI researcher fighting bias

AI researcher Timnit Gebru, the founder of the Distributed AI Research Institute, received her prize for her work in examining how artificial intelligence is influenced by biases.

In a statement, Right Livelihood said she was being honored "for challenging concentrated power in artificial intelligence and pioneering digital technology rooted in justice, lived experience and human agency."

In 2020, Gebru, who was born in Ethiopia to a family of Eritrean origin, was one of the authors behind a paper on the risks of biases in so-called large language models (LLMs) while co-leading tech giant Google's Ethical AI team.

According to the jury, Google dismissed her after she refused to retract the paper or remove her name as requested unless certain guarantees were given.

A Pakistani lawyer fighting repression

Another winner was Jalila Haider of Pakistan, who the jury said was awarded the prize "for breaking barriers, as the first female lawyer from her Hazara community, to challenge ethnic, state and patriarchal persecution, guided by the conviction that no human being is illegal."

Haider is known for her work defending some of her country's most vulnerable communities against repression by the state, discrimination against women and ethnic violence.

"Haider has secured justice for thousands targeted or ignored by those in power, specifically ethnic, gender and religious minorities, as well as refugees," the organization said.

A Southern African rural women's group defending land rights

The Rural Women's Assembly, which brings together more than 178,000 small-scale farmers in 11 Southern African countries, was another winner of the prize.

The Right Livelihood jury said the group had created "a united force defending land, seed and bodily autonomy against corporate and patriarchal dispossession."

Among other things, the Assembly has worked to reproduce and preserve local seed varieties to help protect a long traditional practice of saving and exchanging such seeds, the foundation said.

A Georgian human rights group protecting civic power

The prize also went to the Georgian Young Lawyers' Association (GYLA), which the foundation said it was honoring "as the moral compass of Georgian society."

The jury said the group, founded in 1994, received the award for its efforts in "building and safeguarding Georgian democracy and sustaining civic power in the face of an autocratic crackdown."

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher
